Hi, Gleefre! :D
The Goal section is confusing to me.
So, when scanning `message` from left to right, is every uppercase group of character (/[A-Z]+/) representing Caps Lock being switched?
Like, does "Hello World" becomes "HELLO world" because the "H" turns caps lock on and "W" off? I tried using this logic but it fails at Test 3 'cause "BORDER" would be lower case.
I loved the idea! It's funny :D
Let me know if you manage to solve this one with a regex! Also, let me know if you think this would be a good fit for the reverse mode (but it's probably not).

Hi! yeah, exactly. In the third case "A BORDER" is all typed in with a single shift lock key press, since space isn't affected by shift and thus you don't need to release shift in between. It's covered by the first out of two assumptions in the statement, though it could probably be made clearer (I'm open to wording suggestions!)

Thanks for the feedback, let me see if I can make it clearer, hm...

Would something like this be clearer?

Edit: newer version: "You only press the modifier key <<once>> for each group of consecutive <<uppercase letters>> and <<spaces>>. We assume that <<Caps Lock>> toggles its state immediately after the key is <<pressed>> (and not when it's released.)"

[edit: first version before this edit:] "You only press <<Shift>> (Caps Lock) <<once>> for each group of consecutive <<uppercase letters>> and <<spaces>>. <<Caps Lock>> activates and deactivates when the key is <<pressed>>, not when it's <<released>>."

(Instead of "We assume that for each group of consecutive uppercase letters and spaces, Shift (or, actually, Caps Lock) was pressed only once for the whole group. We also assume that Caps Lock both activates and deactivates when the key is pressed, and not when it is released.")

Ah, thanks! I just changed the Regex in my code from /[A-Z]+/ to /[A-Z ]+/ and now it's working.

I don't know why my mind interpreted "consecutive uppercase letters and spaces" as two different patterns (/[A-Z]+/ and / +/), so I think this was just a misinterpretation of my part.
Ah, I see, hopefully the newer version reads better anyways. Also, did you solve it with regex? I'm guessing (hoping) it at least needs some extra code around it though.

Ooh, I see, you got a variable outside of regex, makes sense. (Nice solution!)

Dunno about the "space isn't affected by shift" phrase, might be nice to include it in the statement, but at the same time it doesn't work quite right without an example / context of the third test case. I think I'm gonna leave it out, at least for now (unless I come up with a better way to phrase it).

Okay, yeah, with an extra variable it's pretty easy to do with regex, if you do it right, got an 58 character solution with ruby & regex. Though handling space correctly is definitely tricky, which is nice :)

P.S. My ruby solution matches against /[a-z ]*[A-Z ]*/, and then flips the caps* variable on each iteration. *actually it's a "swapcase" variable, using ruby's string.swapcase method

58 bytes is insane. I was also trying to code a solution without an extra variable.
After playing around, I could get 104 with JS. I giggled a lot coding this.

print(readline(i=0).replace(/[A-Z ]+|[a-z]/g,c=>(i+=/[A-Z]/.test(c),c[`to${i%2?'Upp':'Low'}erCase`]())))
